passage.title: Stepping into Someone Else's Shoes
paras: When we read a novel, we spend hours inside another person's mind. We hear their thoughts, feel their fears and see the world as they see it, even when they are very different from us.

Many writers and teachers believe this makes reading a training ground for empathy: the ability to understand and share another person's feelings. Some researchers have suggested that readers of fiction do better on tests of understanding others, though scientists still debate how strong the effect is and why.
Literature can also show us people at their worst, and help us understand how ordinary people can be led into cruelty. Reading about it safely, on the page, may make us more alert to it in real life.
Of course, reading alone does not make anyone kind. Empathy grows when we act on what we understand: when we listen, include others and stand up for those who are treated badly.
Perhaps that is the real test of a book: not only whether we enjoyed it, but whether we close it seeing other people a little more clearly.
